subsection: 8. Industrialisation, economic crisis and revolution in Tsarist Russia, 1871–1920

notes.b: Russia was a vast, largely agricultural empire under an autocratic tsar. Serfdom had been abolished only in 1861, and the peasant majority lived in poverty.
points: The Emancipation of 1861 freed the serfs but required peasants to buy land from landlords, often on terms that left them in debt.
Peasants held land in communes (mirs) that shared the land and redistributed it periodically, which discouraged investment and improvement.
Russia had few railways, little heavy industry and a weak banking system in 1871, and it depended heavily on foreign capital and technology.
The autocracy under Alexander II, who was assassinated in March 1881, resisted a constitution, and the bureaucracy and the army dominated government.

notes.b: Sergei Witte, Finance Minister from 1892 to 1903, drove a rapid programme of industrialisation funded by foreign loans and a fixed currency.
points: Witte placed the rouble on the gold standard in 1897, which stabilised the currency and attracted foreign investors.
Foreign loans, mainly from France, financed railway construction and industrial development.
The Trans-Siberian Railway, begun in 1891, linked European Russia with the Pacific port of Vladivostok and was completed in 1916.
Russia's coal, iron and oil industries grew strongly in the 1890s, particularly in the Donbas region of Ukraine and in Baku on the Caspian Sea.
Witte's policy increased the tax burden on peasants and increased the dependence of the economy on foreign capital, which led to criticism from landowners and liberals.

notes.h: The peasant crisis and the 1891 famine
points: Poor harvests in 1891 and 1892 caused a severe famine in the Volga region and other provinces, leading to widespread death and disease.
The government's response was slow and the famine damaged the government's reputation among educated Russians.
Peasants faced rising land hunger and debt, and they resented the redemption payments and the continued power of landlords.
Peasant disorder increased in the years before 1905, with rural protests and attacks on landed estates in several provinces.

notes.h: The Russo-Japanese War and the 1905 revolution
points: The Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905 was fought over control of Manchuria and Korea; Japan attacked Port Arthur in February 1904 without declaring war first.
Port Arthur fell to the Japanese in January 1905, and Russia's Baltic fleet was destroyed at Tsushima in May 1905.
The Treaty of Portsmouth, mediated by President Theodore Roosevelt of the USA and signed in September 1905, ended the war on terms that gave Japan southern Sakhalin and influence in Korea.
On 22 January 1905 troops fired on a peaceful procession led by the priest Georgy Gapon, who was marching to the Winter Palace to present a petition, and this event became known as Bloody Sunday.
Strikes spread across Russia in the autumn of 1905, and the Petersburg Soviet of workers' deputies was formed in October 1905.
Nicholas II issued the October Manifesto on 17 October 1905, which promised civil liberties and an elected Duma with legislative powers.
The Duma was dissolved in July 1906, after the First Duma's demands for land reform and ministerial responsibility, and later Dumas were elected under a franchise that favoured landowners.
The Fundamental Laws of April 1906 preserved the tsar's veto over legislation and his power to rule by decree when the Duma was not in session.

notes.b: Peter Stolypin, Prime Minister from 1906 to 1911, tried to create a class of prosperous independent farmers as the basis of conservative stability.
points: A decree of November 1906 allowed peasants to leave the commune and take their land as private property.
The government's Peasant Land Bank helped peasants buy land, and consolidation of scattered strips into single farms was encouraged.
By about 1914 millions of peasant households had left the communes, but many of the new farms were too small to be profitable.
Stolypin's repression of revolutionaries after 1906 included the use of field courts-martial, which sentenced many people to death.
Stolypin was assassinated in Kiev in September 1911 by a revolutionary who was also a police informer.

notes.h: World War I and the collapse of the autocracy, 1914–1917
points: Russian armies were defeated at Tannenberg in August 1914 and suffered heavy losses in the Masurian Lakes battles.
The Brusilov Offensive of June 1916 briefly restored Russian morale, but it cost very heavy casualties and was not followed up.
Shortages of food, fuel and munitions spread through the cities in 1916 and 1917, and the railways became overloaded and unreliable.
Nicholas II took personal command of the army in September 1915, which made him responsible for military failures and left the government in the hands of his wife Alexandra.
Grigori Rasputin, a holy man who had influence over the imperial family, was murdered by conservative nobles in December 1916, a sign of the regime's collapse.
The February Revolution began on 8 March 1917 in Petrograd with demonstrations by women on International Women's Day, and it spread to the garrison, which joined the crowds.
Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March 1917, and a Provisional Government, which shared power with the Petrograd Soviet, was formed.

notes.h: The October Revolution and the Brest-Litovsk treaty
points: The Bolsheviks, led by Lenin, seized power in Petrograd on 7 November 1917 by storming the Winter Palace and taking control of key government buildings.
Lenin's government issued a decree on peace and a decree on land, promising an end to the war and the transfer of land to the peasants.
The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, signed on 3 March 1918, took Poland, Ukraine and the Baltic provinces out of Russian control.
The Bolsheviks moved the capital to Moscow in March 1918, and in 1918 they introduced War Communism, a policy of requisitioning grain and nationalising industry.
The Cheka, the secret police created in December 1917, carried out executions and arrests of opponents of the Bolsheviks.
The Russian civil war of 1918 to 1920 was fought between the Red Army of the Bolsheviks and the White armies of anti-Bolshevik generals and politicians.
Allied powers, including Britain, France, Japan and the USA, sent troops to support the Whites, but the intervention was small and failed to defeat the Bolsheviks.
The Whites were divided by different aims, and their support was weakened by their lack of popular backing among the peasants.
The Red Army won key victories in 1919 and 1920, and the last White forces in the south were defeated by the end of 1920.
Independence movements in Finland, Poland and the Baltic states were recognised as separate states after the war, and Russia lost much of the territory it had held before 1917.

notes.b: Historians judge the Tsarist regime's economic modernisation both as real progress and as a factor in its downfall.
points: Achievement: Russia's industrial output grew at a rapid rate between 1890 and 1914, and the Trans-Siberian Railway opened up Siberia to settlement.
Limit: industrial growth depended on foreign capital, and it left the peasantry poor and the cities overcrowded and politically volatile.
Achievement: Stolypin's land reforms created a new group of independent farmers and began to change the rural economy.
Limit: the reforms were not completed by 1914, and the war came before they had created the stable rural class that Stolypin wanted.
Achievement: the October Manifesto and the Dumas created a limited parliamentary system in 1905 to 1906.
Limit: the Dumas could not control the government, and the tsar kept power to dismiss ministers and rule by decree.

keyTerms.definition: A war fought across several continents by a large number of states, in which whole societies and economies were mobilised, as in Russia's war from 1914.
The principle that peoples should be able to choose their own government and state, which the Bolsheviks and the Allies applied in different ways after 1917.
The elected Russian parliament created by the October Manifesto of 1905, whose powers were limited by the tsar and the Fundamental Laws of 1906.
The decree of 17 October 1905 in which Nicholas II promised civil liberties and an elected Duma in response to the revolution.
The faction of the Russian Social Democratic Party led by Lenin, which seized power in Petrograd in November 1917.
The treaty of March 1918 by which Soviet Russia left the war and gave up Poland, Ukraine and the Baltic provinces.
The Russian peasant commune, which held land collectively and redistributed it periodically among its households.

factCards.definition: In 1861, under Alexander II, with peasants required to buy land from their former landlords.

factCards.term: When did Russia adopt the gold standard?
factCards.definition: In 1897, under Witte, to stabilise the rouble and attract foreign investment.

factCards.term: When was the Trans-Siberian Railway begun, and when was it completed?
factCards.definition: Begun in 1891 and completed in 1916, linking European Russia with Vladivostok on the Pacific.

factCards.term: When and where did the Russo-Japanese War peace treaty take place?
factCards.definition: The Treaty of Portsmouth, signed in September 1905 after mediation by President Theodore Roosevelt of the USA.

factCards.term: Who led the procession on Bloody Sunday?
factCards.definition: The priest Georgy Gapon, who was marching to present a petition to the tsar at the Winter Palace on 22 January 1905.

factCards.term: What did the November 1906 decree allow peasants to do?
factCards.definition: Leave the commune and take their land as private property, under Stolypin's reforms.
In Kiev in September 1911, by a revolutionary who was also a police informer.
On 15 March 1917, after the February Revolution in Petrograd.

factCards.term: What date did the Bolsheviks seize power in Petrograd?
factCards.definition: 7 November 1917 in the modern calendar, when they stormed the Winter Palace.

factCards.term: What did the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk take away from Russia?
factCards.definition: Poland, Ukraine and the Baltic provinces, which were lost to Russian control.

factCards.term: Which policy did the Bolsheviks adopt in 1918 for grain and industry?
factCards.definition: War Communism, which requisitioned grain from peasants and nationalised industry.
